speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member will please address the Chair, and not the hon. member for Simcoe (Mr. Lennox).

Under the provisions of the Dominion Act disputes were to be settled by the Board of Railway Commissioners; under this Act, there is a very different provision:
In case of any dispute as to the price of power or electrical energy in use or to be provided for use upon the Canadian side of the international boundary line, or the methods of distribution thereof, or the time within which, or the condition on which, the same shall be furnished for use, such dispute shall be settled by the Lieutenant Governor in Council on the application of any applicant for power, or of the company or the town of Fort Francis.
That changes the jurisdiction of this parliament. Under the Dominion Act it is provided that a portion of the power, if it was so ordered by the Board of Railway Commissioners, might be exported for use on the American side under such conditions as the board might impose. Now this Act provides in a different way:
No part of the power or electrical energy to be provided for use on the Canadian side of the said boundary line shall be diverted to or used in the United tSates without the order of the Lieutenant Governor in Council.
Now the Lieutenant Governor, under this statute, takes away from the Board of Railway Commissioners, the power which was given by Dominion statute, and takes to himself to say just what power shall be exported. I want to say to the hon. member that I do not believe the Act is worth the paper it is written on. But, it just goes to show where the question rests. It goes to show that there is a necessity for action on the part of this government with regard to this question. This was an international stream. Why the provincial legislature should have assumed to set aside the Acts of this parliament and to deal with an international and a navigable stream is something that I do not know. It is certainly taking a very extreme course, to say the least about it. But, if hon. gentlemen are questioning the pro-

priety of passing this Act, what have they to say as to the propriety of their friends at Toronto in passing that Act? If these gentleman say, ' You may possibly be invading our rights,' surely they should come here with clean hands. That is a principle of British law and British practice. I will point to only these two Acts, although I could refer to a dozen Acts, in which the same principle was involved. This is a clear case of usurping the authority of the parliament of Canada. Let me give another case in point. Nipigon lake is & large body of water, with about the same coast line as Lake Ontario; yet, the Ontario government have assumed control of it. They have undertaken to forbid anybody to navigate it unless he gets a license from the provincial government. I would like to ask hon. gentlemen where they get any authority for that? If there is anything clear about the British North America Act, if there is anything that is fully established by the statutes of Canada based on that Act, it is that the Dominion has control of navigable waters. Yet, the provincial government assumes to exercise the paramount control over one of the great lakes of the country. Well, I will leave that question for hon. gentlemen to think oveT. Now, what I have to say with regard to this Act, is, that in my humble opinion, it is evidently an Act that should be passed by this legislature. But, I would like to meet the views of my hon. friend the Minister of Justice, and I have this suggestion to make if it will meet with his approval. I recognize that that section 2, which contains a declaration that these works are for the general advantage of Canada, may be open to some objection. Let me say to the committee that this is not at all the Bill that was defeated last year in the Senate. The reason for the defeat in the Senate in part was that the Bill of last year provided for the company going out along all the branches of the Nipigon and Pigeon rivers and erecting storage works for the control of the flow of the water. That has been entirely cut out of the Bill because of the criticism in the Senate Committee. It was pointed out that some of the streams might partake of a different character from either the Nipigon or the Piseon rivers and might not be fairly classed as navigable streams. In view of the force of that statement the clause of last year has been entirely cut out of this Bill, so that, in that respect, it is quite a different Bill. I propose that section 2 shall read in this way: *
Tire works authorized by this Act, in so far only as relates to the development of water powers and electrical transmission, are declared works for the general advantage of Canada.
That would confine it to the two objects alone. I do not know whether that will
meet the views of the Minister of Justice or not, but it seems to me that it would be a very fair declaration. Some hon. gentlemen have asked: 'Why have that declaration at all? What is the purpose of having that declaration?' In answer I may say that this company is proposing to expend a large .sum of money. They will have to go into the money markets and borrow upon their security, no doubt, to carry out their undertaking. They do not want any doubt as to their rights. They do not want any doubt as to whether the Act which they obtain is beyond dispute or not, and m that sense the declaration is regarded as being of some advantage to them. Whether that is a sufficient reason or not I am not prepared to say, but I do say that it is a shield against attack. We see that some of these companies have been dragged into the courts and from court to court under one pretence or another in regard to their charter and the idea was that as a shield against such attacks a declaration, framed as I have just read it, would be of advantage to the company. I cannot see wherein any interest or any individual could possibly be prejudiced by the insertion of that declaration in that section.
Does the hon. gentleman think we could insert in a section like that, the declaration that a certain part of the works are for the general advantage of Canada while excluding a certain other part?

Certainly; you can declare that certain works are for the general advantage of Canada, and if you do not declare that other works are for the general advantage of Canada they will not come within that classification.
But it is part of the same works.

No. This would cut out the manufacturing works. This company propose to create manufacturing establishments. They propose to manufacture pulp and paper and land and marine motors. They would not come under that declaration at all. As I understand the Minister of Justice, if that amendment were not put in all the works of the company might fall under the exclusive jurisdiction of the Dominion. Whether that would prejudice anybody or not I am not prepared to say, but I thought that the amendment which I have submitted would be a pretty fair proposition.

I am sure that the committee has been very gratified to have listened to such an excellent dissertation upon law and fact as we have listened to during the last hour from the hon. member for Thunder bay and Rainy river (Mr. Conmee). He has given to the consideration of these questions a great deal of thought and in his

remarks he has brought to bear upon the consideration of the many matters involved vast experience and learning. But I must confess, Mr. Chairman, that as the hon. gentleman struggled through, as he did in a most able manner' the various intricacies, the constitutional by-ways and the various decisions affecting the .respective rights appertaining to the Dominion and the provinces under the British North America Act, recalling, as the hon. gentleman's remarks did, to my mind, various other statements and arguments that in days long gone by I had heard the hon. gentleman make, both from the public platform and in the legislature of Ontario, of which he was then a member, I was forcibly reminded, Sir, of the story of a western statesman who, having argued volubly from a public platform in favour of the policy which he was advocating, concluded his remarks with these words: ' Now, ladies and gentlemen, these are my views and if you don't like them they can be changed.' The hon. gentleman peculiarly has arguments which, according to time and season and the expediency and exigencies of each situation can be made to adapt themselves as the situation requires. I think that it can be said that there is no question upon which the hon. gentleman has varied his policy and has changed so diametrically his views as he has upon the questions which are involved in and which form the main principles of this Bill. Why, from 1885, when the hon. gentleman first went into the political arena and became a supporter of the late Hon. Sir Oliver Mowat, that doughty champion of provincial rights, whose policy the hon. gentleman so loyally followed-
And still follows.

Yes, and still follows, the hon. gentleman in every campaign in which he was following loyally declared in favour of provincial rights, everything for the provinces, the mines, the lumber, the licenses, the fisheries, the surrendered Indian lands -everything should go to the provinces, including the water-powers. But a change suddenly came over the spirit of the dreams of the hon. gentleman. It was not a gradual change, it came suddenly, almost in a night, and that was the night of the 25th day of January, 1905. Why, Sir, from 1886 until the night of the 25th of January, 1905, the hon. gentleman from Thunder Bay and Rainy River (Mr. Conmee) had the most implicit confidence in the fullest possible powers of the legislature of the province of Ontario to pass such legislation and to control companies of this kind which were exclusively within their jurisdiction. What do we find? The first step the hon. gentleman took was with regard to a company with which he was intimately connected, of which he was an in-Mr. BOYCB.
corporator and provisional director and which from 1886 to 1904 had been incorporated and kept exclusively within the jurisdiction and control of the province of Ontario.
What company was that?
That was the Pacific and Atlantic Railway Company.
Oh.
Yes, yes, yes.
I would like to know what the Pacific and Atlantic Railway Company has got to do with this.

My hon. friend from 1886 to 1905 laboured, I presume, under the delusion, as he would have us now believe, that these matters were within the legislative control exclusively of the province of Ontario. He secured the incorporation of that company in an Act of the Ontario legislature which gave it very large powers. He renewed that charter and renewed it, and renewed it, without having performed one of its stipulations. Session after session he secured from the legislature of Ontario unconditional renewals of the powers granted by this Act until this awful calamity happened on the 25th of January, 1905. After that calamity he knocked but once more at the doors of the legislature and he was met with the condition that he must proceed with the work and must spend $300,000 in one year. What did he do? Not one single thing to carry out the conditions.
I rise to a point of order. The hon. gentleman is addressing his remarks to me. I had nothing to do with the railway company of which he speaks for more than 20 years.
Except as an incorporator, a provisional director.
My name was used on one or two occasions. I never had a dollar's interest in it, I never was a promoter, I was never anything more to the company than the member who introduced the Bill.

I was proceeding to say that the moment the Ontario legislature, as constituted in 1905, directed the company to do something to carry out the objects of incorporation and spend $300,000 in one year, the company, without having done one single thing, without having spent a dollar as ordered by the legislature, came to the parliament of Canada of which the hon. gentleman was then a member, and he said: 'This is a matter entirely and exclusively within the control of the Dominion parliament, it must

be relegated to Dominion jurisdiction and there it must stay,' and that railway, which for all these years, had nestled snugly and safely in the lap of the provincial legislature, the moment something was to he done, the moment terms were imposed by the Tory administration, the hon. gentleman comes here and says:
' Jurisdiction over this company must be taken away from the province of Ontario and it must be declared a work for the general advantage of Canada.' The hon. gentleman argued from his place that the work mentioned in that Bill was a work for the general benefit of the Dominion of Canada, and he gave no other excuses for the non-performance of the conditions imposed by the legislature of Ontario in regard to promoting and safeguarding the interests of the public than that it had suddenly grown, by reason of this awful calamity, a work for the general advantage of Canada and this House so declared it.
Does the hon. gentleman say I was an incorporator of that company?
Yes, I say he was that.
If the hon. gentleman looks at the Act he will find he is mistaken.
Has he the document?
No.
Neither have I.
Then he should not make the statement.
I have made the statement before and you never denied it.
I deny it now.
I accept the hon. gentleman's denial.
I understood the hon. member to say that I was one of the incorporators of the company when it came here. I was not one of the promoters, not when it came here.

I did not say that. I do not want to do any injustice. I say that the hon. gentleman was one of the original incorporators and directors of that company when it was originally incorporated in the Ontario legislature.

I understood the hon. gentleman to say ' then what did the hon. gentleman do? He came down to this House,'-and then he went on to state what I had done here. I had nothing to do with the Bill for many years before it came here. Mr. Clergue and his companies had control of it.

I accept entirely the hon. gentleman's explanation of what happened
after the incorporation of the company. This is one of the questions on which the hon. gentleman who has become an authority on these great constitutional questions, has changed his views. There are others. We listened to a learned disquisition on this subject from the Minister of Justice, and while the hon. member for Thunder Bay (Mr. Conmee) did not agree with the Minister of Justice in all respects, he went a little further in some respects. The hon. gentleman said in this House that this Nipigon river was an international stream.
No.

Was international in its character. At page 1068 of ' Hansard ' the hon. member said:
The Pigeon river is an international water and the Nipigon is a navigable water, and, in my opinion, also international in character.
Then at page 1069 we find:
That is an international water.
Certainly, so is the Nipigon river, to a certain extent at least, in my opinion.
Not seriously?

Yes, I am quite serious, and I am quite prepared to back up my opinion with sufficient evidence.
That was on the 15th of February, 1909, upon this very same Bill, and yet the hon. gentleman now argues solemnly before this committee that the Nipigon river is not an international stream, but that as a navigable stream it should be subject to the jurisdiction of this parliament.
The hon. gentleman will pardon me for a moment. He has made the statement that I stated in the House that the Nipigon river was an international stream.
I read the hon. gentleman's remarks in ' Hansard.'
It does not matter what the hon. gentleman has read from ' Hansard.' I never made the statement. Another thing, I cannot find those words in * Hansard.' The hon. member for Hastings repeated-
I gave place to the hon. member to ask a question, not to make a speech.
If the hon. member wants to insist on that sort of buncombe, I suppose he can do it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member should not use an expression of that kmd.
Take it back.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I did not say that it was necessary for the hon. member to withdraw the expression. I think that much liberty of expression the Chairman has. I called his attention to it as an inappropriate expression, but it does not follow that on all occasions such expressions must be withdrawn.

The hon. gentleman seems to be very scrupulous. I said I did not want to do him any injustice, and I quoted his words from 'Hansard'; and yet the hon. gentleman gets up and says he did not use those words and cannot find them. I will give him the pages-1068 and 1069, dated February the 15th, unrevised ' Hansard.' The first ground the hon. gentleman took to argue himself into a position to assert that this parliament and no other should have jurisdiction over the Nipigon river was that it was an international water -international in character; I suppose he means of international reputation. I think the hon. gentleman's remarks this afternoon have sufficiently disposed of that argument. Now, the hon. gentleman argues that by reason of the Nipigon river being a navigable river, this parliament should have jurisdiction over it. I take issue with my hon. friend upon that point; and in the next place, conceding for the sake of argument that the Nipigon river may be considered to be a navigable river for the purposes of this Act, the legislature of Ontario has full legislative jurisdiction. Looking at a sketch of the Nipigon river which I have I see that very close to the mouth, of the river there are rapids, and that the river is navigable for a distance of only about three miles beyond those rapids until there is another rapid; that is, it is navigable in the sense of being deep enough for boats to travel between those two points. From there on it is not in any sense a navigable river. But if we concede for the sake of argument that the two or three miles between those two rapids make of the Nipigon river a navigable stream, what then? My hon. friend has quoted voluminously and learnedly from a case in law to establish the fact that where there is a navigable stream, the jurisdiction of the province must perforce cease; but there is where I must take issue with the hon. gentleman, and upon the very case which he has cited. He quotes from the decision of the Privy Council in the fisheries case, reported in Appeal Cases of 1898, at page 700. Lord Herschel was one of _ the Lords Justices who delivered judgment in that case, and this is what he said at page 714;-and I commend it to the mature deliberation of my hon. friend from Thunder Bay and Rainy River, because he must have omitted this paragraph from the judgment which he read:
Lord Herschel expressed the view that R.S.O., 1887, chap. 24, sec. 47, is within the Mr. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
legislative authority of Ontario, except so far as ooncerns lands in public harbours and canals, if any of the latter be included. This section authorizes the Lieutenant Governor to make sales or appropriations of ' land covered with water in the harbours, rivers and other navigable waters in Ontario, under such conditions as it has been or it may be deemed requisite to impose, but not so as to interfere with the use of any harbour as a harbour, or with the navigation of any harbour, river or other navigable waters.'
That is a part of the dictum in the fisheries case. Where does that leave my hon. friend? There is no part of the Nipigon river which the hon. gentleman proposes to develop under this power Bill which can by any stretch of imagination be said to be navigable. Nothing that the Ontario legislature could do in the exercise of its legislative jurisdiction could possibly interfere with the navigation of that river. My hon. friend must therefore see that where there is no interference by the actual exercise of jurisdiction by the local legislature, there is no clash of jurisdiction with the Dominion parliament, and the matter rests solely within the jurisdiction of the provincial legislature. But my hon. friend has experienced, even in this connection, and it is lamentable to notice it, a great change of heart-a great reversal of judgment; and I cannot understand why he should have reversed his judgment when he thought that the judgment he expressed to-day was so much in line with what Lord Herschel and the Lords Justices had said in deciding the fisheries case. The hon. gentleman's argument to-day was in line with the way in which he read the fisheries case, when he said that where there was a navigable river and where the works proposed to be constructed would interfere -with the navigation of that river, then the jurisdiction passed to this parliament. After first approving of that decision of the Privy Council, after removing for all time any doubt as to what their lordships really meant, after having given the people of Canada his dictum as to what was in their lordships' mind, when they gave that judgment, although not expressed in it, my hon. friend said- and I refer to his remarks because they are very pertinent in this connection. They will be found on page 66697 of ' Hansard,' June 30, 1906:
Whatever power is available for the Canadian side is a question entirely within the jurisdiction of the Ontario government, first, as regards the use of the bed of the river for that purpose, and second, of this government as regards the use of the stream, because it ir an international stream.
Does the hon. gentleman say that to-day?

Certainly. I have never argued that the provincial government had not rights. But what I say is that whatever rights they have, whether in an inter-

national stream or a navigable stream, are not interfered with by this Bill.
The quotation I have read refers to the St. Mary's river, which undoubtedly is an international stream, and in that connection he says you have to go to Ontario in order to get your rights.
Not at all.

The hon. gentleman said:
Whatever power is available for the Canadian side is a question entirely within the jurisdiction, as I understand it, first, of the Ontario government as regards the use of the bed of the river

The hon. gentleman was talking about the St. Mary's river, which is an international and navigable stream, and he says that the first thing you have to do is to go to the Ontario government because it owns the bed of the stream.
If the hon. gentleman will only use my words and not enlarge on them the committee will understand him better.
I must ask my hon-. friend to allow me to retain the floor.
Go on and make all the misrepresentations you please.
I rise to a point of order. The hon. gentleman must withdraw those words.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member has no right to charge misrepresentation, and I hope he will withdraw the expression.
Surely no one is obliged to sit and listen to another misrepresenting his words without making some protest.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has no right to make comments on my ruling, but must withdraw the expression which I have ruled out of OTder.
I said that I never made use of the words the hon. gentleman attributed to me, and under the rules of the House he is bound to take my word.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has the right to make an explanation on the point of order, but not to make a speech or any lengthy remarks.

What I say is that I never used the language the hon. gentleman has attributed to me. I went on to correct him and he objected. I never used the language or contended for the principle he imputes to me.
The hon. gentleman said to the hon. member for Algoma that he could go on and make misrepresentations to any extent he saw fit.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: That was the expression I thought not in order, and the hon. gentleman must withdraw both the use of the word ' you,' thus addressing a member directly insisted of the Chair, and the charging of an hon. member with misrepresentation.

I bow, Sir, to your ruling, but let me ask that the rules of the House be enforced equally against all members. I rose in my place and said I had not used the words which the hon. gentleman cited as mine, and he continued to repeat them, and was not called to order. I ask now that he be called to ordeT regarding the statement he has made.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It is too late now to raise a point of order with regard to words uttered some time ago. Had I noticed any unparliamentary words I would have had them withdrawn, but my attention was not called to any such. I understand that the hon .member for Rainy River has withdrawn the expression I ruled out of order.

You state, Sir, that the hon. gentleman has withdrawn the expressions. I have read the hon. gentleman's words as they appear in the records of the House. The hon. gentleman stood up and said he did not use these words.

I ask the hon. gentleman to withdraw that statement. I have no objection to his reading any words I have uttered, but what I do object to is the misrepresentation he applies to them. What I object to is his misrepresentation of my words and not to his reading them.

I was proceeding to state that the position which the hon. gentleman found it then expedient to take was a position, as appears by his own words, that in St. Mary's river, an international, navigable stream, whatever powers are there available for the Canadian side come entirely within the jurisdiction, first, of the Ontario government as regards the bed of the river, and secondly, of this government, as regards the use of the water. He could not have made use of a broader example, because, if there be any stream in Canada in which there would be an interference by the provincial government in the exercise of what it conceived to be its legislative jurisdiction, it would be that river because it combines the two elements about which my hon. friend has argued separately. Because, in the Nipigon river he has, according to his own contention, a navigable, but-contrary to his own contention on the same Bill a few days ago- not an international stream; and in the Pigeon river, he has an international, though I understand that he does not argue it to be a navigable stream.
I argued that both were navigable.

Then, I misunderstood the hon. gentleman. But, as I say, the hon. gentleman has stated as strong a case as possible for the contention that where you have an international and navigable stream, you must go to the provincial legislature for whatever power you require. And therefore I say to him now that I accept his word as contained in that argument, and I say that is the place for him to go and that is where he ought to be.

I again call attention to the hon. member's (Mr. Boyce's) course. In the language which he read, I merely stated that the ownership, or control if you choose to use the word, of the bed of the river was in the provincial government, and the hon. gentleman continues to misrepresent in that respect.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Conmee) did not say that. In order that he may not forget the words to which I have referred, I will read them again:
Whatever power is available for the Canadian side is a question entirely within the jurisdiction, as I understand it, first, of the Ontario government as regards the use of the bed of the river for that purpose; and, second, of this government as regards the use of the water, because it is an international stream, and I assume they would have to get the consent of this government.
At six o'clock, committee took recess.
After Recess.
Committee resumed at eight o'clock.

When you left the Chair, Mr. Chairman, I was proceeding to discuss the question of a navigable water as affecting the question of jurisdiction, and as being one of the excuses which the hon. member who is promoting this Bill has put forth, supported by the Minister of Justice, for interference with what I conceive to be the exclusive jurisdiction of the province of Ontario in this case, and of other provinces in cases of a similar nature. The main contention of my hon. friend, as I understand, is that because the Nipigon and Pigeon rivers are navigable to some extent, any works for the development of power, or any works which in any way encroach upon these navigable rivers, would be beyond the jurisdiction of the province, and therefore ultra vires of its legislature. Now I do not understand that there is any longer any virtue in that argument, I understand that such arguments have been at least discussed by the fisheries case, and disposed of by another case with which I suppose my hon. friend is familiar, that is the case of Me-1 Mr. BOYCE.
Millan vs. South West Boom Company, reported in 2 Cartwright, page 542. The gist of that decision is that the fact that a river is navigable does not in itself alone transfer that river to the Dominion jurisdiction. That is the gist of the decision in the McMillan case, and it runs through the Fisheries case, as I have shown, and is in accordance, as I understand it, with the views laid down by my hon. friend himself three years ago. If I were to go further along the line I was following before recess, I would point out to my hon. friend the position in which he found himself when he advocated that principle. He was asking this parliament to declare as a work for the general benefit of Canada a railway company which was incorporated in Ontario and continued to be under provincial jurisdiction. I know he will remember, and that other members of the committee will remember, the strenuous objection that was raised from this side of the House on the ground that the declaration of that work as one for the general advantage of Canada would seriously interfere with provincial jurisdiction, and would deprive the province of certain water-powers which were in a state of semi-development on that river, iviy hon. friend's contention, in order to get his measure 'through, was this: ' We cannot take your water-powers, we are not interfering with your water-powers; if we wished to interfere with your water-powers we could not for the reason '-and the reason is given in the quotation I made to my hon. friend of his own words-' that these water-powers are entirely within the jurisdiction, first, of the province of Ontario as regards the river bed, and secondly, of this parliament as regards the question of an international stream.' Now my hon. friend has said that these are powers which should not be given by the Ontario legislature, that they aTe powers ultra vires of the1 Ontario legislature. My answer to that is what my hon. friend announced as his principle on the 30th day of June, 1905, and that he had consistently adhered to prior to that time; because I find on reference to the Acts of the Ontario legislature so far back as 1886, which was the year after my hon. friend first entered public life and became a legislator in this country, that he introduced a measure, or was the promoter of a measure, called the Ontario & Rainy River Railway Company, incorporated by chapter 75 of the Ontario Act of 1886, and I commend to my hon. friend the reading of some of the powers which are given to that company by that Act. It was an Ontario railway which was promoted towards Rat-Portage, and by section 33, these powers were given to that company:
It shall and may be lawful for the company at any point where the railway, or any

branch thereof, approaches within two miles of any navigable waters, to purchase and hold as its absolute property, and for the use of the company, wharfs, piers, docks, water lots, water frontages, and lands; and upon the said water lots, water frontages and lands, and in and over the waters adjoining the same, to build and erect elevators, storehouses, warehouses and engine houses, sheds, wharfs, docks, piers and other erections.
' On navigable waters,' which are as my hon. friend contends now, absolutely and exclusively within the jurisdiction of this parliament. So we find the hon. gentleman, during the time the late Hon. Mr. Mowat was Prime Minister of Ontario, promoting and advocating a Bill and getting it carried into law, giving to this company all sorts of powers which are exercised upon navigable waters. Well, if I wanted to elaborate and multiply instances, I might also refer my hon. friend to the Bill incorporating the Pacific and Atlantic Railway Company, the very railway which we were discussing before Tecess. Section 6 of the Act, which is chapter 76 of the Ontario statutes of 1886, gives the company power:
To purchase, lease, or acquire at any point where their railway or any branch thereof touches, or approaches within two miles of any navigable waters, sufficient land for the uses of the company, their railway and vessels run or navigated in connection with said railway, and the company may erect warehouses, elevators, docks, wharfs, stations, workshops, and such other buildings as may be necessary for the purposes of the company, and may sell and convey such land as may be found superfluous for any such purposes.
These are similar powers to those given to the Ontario & Rainy River Railway Company. My hon. friend admitted that he was the promoter of this Bill. I also noticed that by section 1, one J. Conmee is an incorporator of the company and a provisional director. So that my hon. friend was doing
When was that?
Oh.
Do I understand my hon. friend to say that that was not he?
No, I was only asking the date. Go ahead; it is all right.

1886. So that what my hon. friend was doing, in the Ontario legislature in 1886, a year after he came into public life, when he had drawn the first innocent breaths of his political career, before he had become contaminated by his associations and by different spheres of activity-
Be careful now.

What he was doing, as the promoter of a Bill of which he himself was incorporator and a provisional director, was exactly what he now says the Ontario legislature has no power to do, namely, to give power to construct works upon navigable waters. The other excuse that my hon. friend puts forward, and one which was emphasized very strongly by the Minister of Justice, had reference to the right given to this company to export power. I must confess that it was a somewhat shocking and sweeping proposition for the Minister of Justice to say that because this company purported to have power to export its surplus product to the United States, the Ontario legislature was deprived of jurisdiction to legislate with reference to this matter and that therefore the question was brought exclusively within the jurisdiction of this parliament. I was not absolutely certain that that was what the Minister of Justice meant to say and I sent him over a written question in order that I might be sure. He read that question over and sent an answer in the affirmative. Let us see where that leads us. Because there is inserted in any Dominion Bill introduced on behalf of a company seeking power to export its surplus product to the United States the Ontario legislature is deprived of jurisdiction. What is to prevent any power company under the sun from coming to this House, putting in its Bill the right to export its surplus product and thus take away from the province of Ontario every vestige of power rights it has? I think this committee will desire something more weighty from the Minister of Justice than a proposition like that. It certainly does not appeal to me as being founded on sound common sense from the legal point of view, and it is certainly not such an opinion as we should expect to receive from that hon. gentleman. But it does seem to me that if ever there was a paltry, flimsy excuse by which the jurisdiction that the Ontario government is exercising with regard to the power question can be stolen from it the Minister of Justice gave it to this committee this afternoon in the speech which he made.
Now, I want to refer for a moment to some of the Ontario legislation with respect to poweT. I will first refer to the Act which was passed by the Ontario legislature respecting water-powers in 1898. By that Act, Chapter 8, the commissioner of Crown lands was given power to:
Reserve from sale any water-power or privilege on the Crown lands of the province, and a sufficient area of land in connection therewith for the erection of buildings and plant, together with the right to lay out and use such roads as may be necessary for passage to and from such water-power or privi-

lege and land, and may under regulations to be approved by the Lieutenant Governor in Council, make terms and conditions upon which such water-power and land so reserved may be sold, or leased, and developed.
That was assented to on the 17th January 1889. At that time the hon. member for Thunder Bay and Rainy River was a supporter of the government in the Ontario legislature, and I do not know that he lifted up his voice or made any very strenuous objection to the Ontario government exercising control over the waters or over the bed of the river when they took that course. Then again, following the history of Ontario legislation in regard to power, we find an Act passed in 1903, just before the late government went out of power. That was an Act providing for the construction of municipal power works and the transmission, distribution and supply of electrical and other power and energy. I shall not take up the time of the committee by reading it at length, but I would commend to my hon. friend and to other members of the committee the full powers which are given to the municipal commission under this Act for the acquisition and the control of power rights. Then, we find that the present government, in the year 1906, introduced an Act which was passed by the legislature of Ontario, being chapter 15, and entitled 'An Act to provide for the transmission of electrical power to municipalities'; otherwise known as the HydroElectric Power Commission Act. It gave certain powers to a commission to examine into, to inquire and to report upon water-powers in the province of Ontario. By section 11 that Act provides :
The commission may, from time to time, report to the Governor in Council, designating such lands, water privileges, water-powers or the lands, works, machinery and plant, or any portion thereof of any company or person owning, or holding under lease or otherwise, or developing, operating or using any water privilege or water-power, or transmitting electrical or other power or energy in the province of Ontario which should, in the opinion of the commission, be purchased, acquired, leased, taken or expropriated, developed, operated or used by the commission for the purposes of this Act, or may designate what quantity of the product of any such corporation or individual developing electrical power or energy in the province of Ontario, or purchasing such power or energy the commission requires for the purposes of this Act.
Again, by section 12, the Lieutenant-Governor was authorized:
to acquire by purchase, lease or otherwise, or without the consent of the owners thereof, or persons interested therein to enter upon, take and use the lands, works, plant and property of any company or person owning, using and developing or operating lands, water, water privileges, or works, plant and 1

machinery for the development of any water privilege or water-power for the purpose of generating electrical power or energy, or for the transmission thereof in the province of Ontario, and to develop and supply electrical power or energy.
That was an absolute legislative assertion of the right of the province of Ontario to deal with and to exercise control of, to expropriate and to manage exclusively any water-powers in the province of Ontario and to control the rates. That power policy has been approved of by the people of Ontario and is now being carried out by the government of that province to the great and lasting benefit of the people. The power commission appointed by the Ontario government made a special report with regard to the water-powers in the Algoma, Thunder Bay and Rainy River districts. In that report the very water-power sought to be acquired by this company is dealt with as a part of the power policy of the Ontario government. At page 17 of the commission's fifth report there is a reference to the Cameron Rapids development, the very power which my hon. friend in committee admitted this company proposed to use. How then could this parliament authorize a company to utilize that power without a direct clash of authority?
Section 8 of this Bill provides:
The company may-
(a) acquire, develop, improve, maintain and operate water-powers, use, supply and sell water-power for any purpose, by any means of application, generate, by means of waterpower or otherwise, electricity, heat, light and any other form of energy, and transmit the same by any means to, and supply and sell the same for use in any manner at, any place in Canada and the United States.
The one point on the Nipigon river is the very point referred to in the report of the Ontario Hydro-Electric Commission.
The last report of the Waterways Commission, which is a Dominion commission, expressly seeks to prevent the giving away of any further water-powers until such time as a thorough examination shall be made as to their extent and development. Supplementing that I would quote from a newspaper account of a very interesting lecture delivered here by Professor Shortt before the Canadian Society of Civil Engineers, on ' Water-powers.' The keynote to his address was: ' Keep your water-powers, do not give them away or dissipate them now because therein lies the future welfare of the manufacturing industries of this country.' May I quote from the report of Professor Shortt's address in the Ottawa ' Citizen ' of April 5:
The people of Canada were beginning to wake up to the fact that the resources of the country werre being rapidly depleted and from this awakening the movement for the conservation of resources had sprung. The recent conference at Washington had been a very

hopeful sign, and the document sent to Canada as the result was a wise one. It was Gtal that the idea of conserving resources should be brought home to the individual realization of the people of the continent. The steps already taken should be augmented by the full awakening of public sentiment.
The water resources of Canada were of special importance on account of the immense economic possibilities of the water regions of the country.
Professor Shortt is an eminent authority upon economic questions and has devoted a great deal of study to the question of our natural resources. It will be a serious handicap to our industrial development if the government continues to give away our water-powers.
We were told in one of the committees of the House the other day by a gentleman who was called before that committee as an expert that the National Transcontinental Railway Commission had now under consideration the electrifying of their railway right in this Nipigon region. It is the most expensive part of the railway to run, the part where fuel is most difficult to get, and the part where the cost of operation will be most heavy. Therefore, it is surely veTy much in the interest of the people of Canada that the cost of operating that railway should be minimized as much as possible. But if the largest waterpower in that district, the Cameron Rapids, is given to a private corporation, where is the benefit of that power to the people of Canada? Where is the opportunity for the National Transcontinental Railway Commissioners in the future, ten or twenty years from now, to give to the people of Canada on that portion of the railway which is being built for and will be owned by the people of Canada, the advantage of lessening the cost of operation of the railway, which will be enormous in any event? The future of the towns on the great lakes is a manufacturing future. Large manufacturing industries will undoubtedly be established there, it may be in a very short time. The natural fuel there is white coal, from the water-powers which nature has so lavishly bestowed on that country, and if we are to have, as we all hope we shall have, large manufacturing centres established on the great lakes, what greater impetus can there be to the easy and expeditious establishment of such industries than the fact that we are conserving the magnificent water-powers which will give the power to turn the wheels of those great industries? My hon. friend from North Grey (Mr. Mid-dlehro) has just placed in my hands an extract from an address before the Ottawa Canadian Club on this subject by Mr. Gifford Pinchot, in which he said: "
Coal will be finished by the middle of the next century. High grade iron ores, oil and gas will disappear by the middle of this
century. Waste by erosion of lands easily prevented was incalculable. Forests were not*" producing anything like what they should; of every 1,000 board feet of lumber in the woods only 310 was made into lumber. The reasonably available water-power in the United States could operate every railway, run every trolley car, light every home, turn every spindle in the country. If coal disappeared at once, water-power could easily take its place. The commission (the International Conservation Commission of the United States) found that these water-powers were fast becoming controlled by far-sighted capitalists. If this were carried on the nation would find itself, when coal was used up, at the mercy of the greatest monopoly ever formed in the world. For when fuel disappears for motive power, heat and light, every one must go to the water-power for it.
There is one of the most cogent hints ever given by a man well versed in the subject to this government to conserve the water-powers and to refuse to put the water-powers of our country under the control of capitalists and corporations. Now, a word with regard to the position taken by the hon. Minister of Justice. That hon. gentleman, in a speech delivered in this House during this session, stated that his party was the champion of provincial rights. In contrast with the attitude taken by the hon. minister upon this Bill, his prior statement is open to some exception. He virtually tacitly assents to the measure now before this committee, which takes from the legislative control of the province of Ontario the whole of the bed of the Nipigon river and half of the bed of the Pigeon river, upon the legal or legislative fiction, first, that these rivers are at those points navigable waters, and, secondly, that power is to be exported to the United States of America in each case. Both of those arguments could be applied to every river and stream in the province of Ontario. If it is because the Nipigon river is navigable for two miles, several miles below the point at which my hon. friend's company proposes to take its power, that this government claims jurisdiction, as in the ease of the Pigeon river, the same legislative fiction could be applied to every river and stream in the province of Ontario, because at some point or other every river and stream can be said to be navigable by the application of the same logic by which my hon. friend reaches the conclusion that the Nipigon river and the Pigeon river are navigable. Then you have no reason for denying to any company the right to come to this parliament and ask for the water-powers on any stream or river in Ontario. My hon. friend has referred to the Bill respecting the Ontario and Minnesota Power Company. If the hon. gentleman had carefully considered the situation before he cited that Bill as a part of his case, he would have hesitated. Let us see where it would land him. My

hon. friend is claiming that this parliament has power and that the legislature of Ontario has no power to give to the Ontario and Michigan Power Company the right to own, control, develop and operate water-powers on the Pigeon and Nipigon rivers. He cites the case of the Ontario and Minnesota Power Company, which in the year 1905 came to this parliament to ask by private legislation for certain powers. My hon. friend was the promoter of that Bill, and certain powers were granted subject to certain conditions.

No, I was not the promoter. I opposed the Bill.
Mr!. BOYCE. That legislation passed and certain powers were granted over an international stream practically along the lines of this Bill. My hon. friend referred to it as a precedent for the very legislation he is now introducing.
I did not cite the case of the Ontario and Minnesota Power Bill as a justification for this measure, but as a case in which the interests of the people were not guarded by provincial legislation.

That legislation passed, and in the year 1906, we find that company going to the Ontario legislature for the Act to which my hon. friend has referred. Why did it go to the Ontario government after having come here?
They went there to escape the obligations which this parliament imposed upon them in the interests of the people. *

I accept, so far as it goes, my hon. friend's explanation, but I do not know that it places him in any better position. They went because it was contended that the company was not bound by the conditions imposed by this parliament but was entitled to deal with the waterpower free from the restrictions imposed by the Dominion Act. What is the provincial legislation which was granted ? Clause 1 gives the company the right to provide power on the Canadian side of the river. Subsection 2 provides that the works shall be on the Canadian side. Subsection 3 provides for the settlement of any dispute regarding the rates to be charged for the power, bringing the whole question back within the jurisdiction of the provincial legislation. In answer to my hon. friend from South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) my hon. friend said that the Ontario government were usurping the jurisdiction of this parliament in passing that Bill.
Yes.
He further said that that Act was ultra vires the province of Ontario. The Minister of Justice made a I

similar argument this afternoon. If what he said was the case with regard to the Ontario and Minnesota Power Company, as it should be with the Ontario and Michigan Power Company, that Act was ultra vires the province of Ontario. But did we hear of any application for disallowance? Did my hon. friend make any such application? Why did he, with all his knowledge of constitutional questions, not suggest to the Minister of Justice that that Act was ultra vires of the province of Ontario and a usurpation by that province of the rights of this parliament? I do_ not know that the argument of the Minister of Justice could have any more conclusive answer than my hon. friend has given him in the case he cited of the Ontario and Minnesota Power Company, because if there be any virtue in the argument of the Minister of Justice or of my hon. friend, the Ontario government had no power to pass that Act and it should have been disallowed. However, it was not disallowed and remains to-day as law, although to-day it is recognized as a usurpation of the jurisdiction of this parliament by that same minister, before whom it came up in order to determine whether it was a proper Act for the Ontario legislature to pass or not. He must therefore be assumed to have passed upon its validity and to have recognized that the Ontario government had the power to control the water in an international and navigable stream. Consequently his action in that matter negatives his argument today.
One more word and I am glad to see the right hon. the Prime Minister in his place. The right hon. gentleman has adopted the policy of the conservation of our natural resources. But the most important of those is our water-powers. Is he going, notwithstanding the warnings of men like Prof. Shortt and Mr. Pinchot and the speeches made by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher), to allow the water-powers of this country to be given over to the control of corporations, which will thereby obtain vested rights in them to the great disadvantage of our people, particularly in the future when our New Ontario will have blossomed as the rose. Of what use will be the committee which the right hon. gentleman has appointed on our forests, waterways and water-powers, unless such questions as this are to be brought before it? Why could not this Bill be referred to that committee? I again appeal to him to carry out his policy of conservation and to stick to his principle of provincial rights. There is here a very serious conflict of jurisdiction from which he cannot escape. The Ontario government takes control of certain powers in certain rivers and streams in Ontario and provides for the regulating and developing of those

powers and the rates that shall be charged the public for their use. That policy is a popular one endorsed by the people of that province. This Bill cannot be regarded as other than a direct and flagrant interference with that policy and an attempt to wrest from the province of Ontario the jurisdiction given it by our constitution, by our laws, by the precedents of our judges in contested cases, and by the right of user. Therefore, I say to the right hon. the Prime Minister that I sincerely hope, before he allows this Bill to go, either now in committee or before it has received its third reading, he will consider well these two questions, the question of provincial rights, and the question of conservation of our natural national resources, that he will look to the future, and will stay this Bill with what I conceive to be its ini-quitious provisions and the extraordinary powers it grants.

There has been a great deal of argument on this Bill which we should take very seriously into consideration. I do not think I shall go into the question, interesting as it is, of jurisdiction. I think that has been presented so very well from this side of the House that it is almost useless to argue it further. Of course I was very much interested in the elaborate argument of the hon. member (Mr. Conmee) who is promoting the Bill. It is always interesting to hear him speak, and especially to hear him deal with questions of law. In fact, we had rather a rare treat this afternoon, because we had first the learned and clever argument of the Minister of Justice (Hon. Mr. Aylesworth) which I think I can compliment myself on having elicited, and then we had the speech of what I may call the junior counsel, the hon. member for Thunder Bay and Rainy River (Mr. Conmee). It is always particularly interesting to hear him deal, with such complete confidence as he shows with legal questions, especially those questions that are probably more difficult than any others, the questions of jurisdiction between the province and the Dominion. I am sorry that I cannot transfer to 'Hansard' and embalm in its pages a very pretty little picture I clipped some time ago from the Toronto 'Telegram.' It expresses the situation very nicely. It shows upon the platform the hon. gentleman who is promoting this Bill-an excellent likeness of him, as any one who looks at the picture will recognize-He is in an eloquent attitude, and fortified with a glass and pitcher-I presume, of water-and evidently intends to discuss the question at any length as he discussed this afternoon the question of law. Sir J. P. Whitney is figuratively at the feet of this Gamaliel, below the platform. He ventures a suggestion, 'You cannot give a charter contrary to provincial rights.' Sir. J. P.
Whitney has not been in the House of Commons, or he would recognize that that is limiting our power very decidedly, and that we can and that we do grant charters contrary to provincial rights. But my hon. friend from Thunder Bay and Rainy River sets Sir J. P. Whitney right, and expresses the situation in a few words. I may say that the Minister of Justice (Hon. Mr. Aylesworth) is represented in the picture also, in a somewhat less conspicuous attitude than the hon. member for Thunder Bay and Rainy River, and a very excellent likeness of the Minister of Justice it is as well. To Sir J, P. Whitney replies James Conmee, J.P., M.P., expressing himself much to the same effect as he did this afternoon:	'If me and me learned friend
Brother Aylesworth read the British North America Act aright, we kin give a man a charter to take the furnace out of your cellar for the general advantage of Canada.'

speechtext: It is not allowable to characterize any proceeding of this House as 'a roaring farce.'

I withdraw 'roaring farce,' Mr. Chairman. It would be a roaring farce if it were outside. But I may be permitted to say that we can carry to an absurd length the practice of constantly objecting to statements made in the House. The matter I have referred to concerning my hon. friend (Mr. Conmee) is such that a man has to be very sensitive and thin-skinned indeed-my hon. friend is a very sensitive gentleman, I presume-to feel hurt or injured by it. I do not know anybody who could be more perturbed than I would be if I intentionally caused any worry to the hon. gentleman. I recognize that he has the greatest consideration for every hon. member on this side of the House, and it would be very bad taste on my part to say anything that would cause him annoyance. I hope he will not object to my paying him a little special attention, if he would so designate it, in reference to his Bill-without any covert meaning on the word 'special' either. But I regard his Bill as of sufficient importance to call for very careful attention, not to say special attention, on the part of hon members of this House.
Now, I said I would not discuss the question of jurisdiction. But I want to say as distinctly as I can that it is our duty to consider his measure very carefully from the point of view of policy. If you admit that we have jurisdiction to pass this Bill, still, as the Minister of Justice said this afternoon, there remains the great question whether it is judicious, expedient, wise, to enact this legislation, and it is from that point of view, Mr. Chairman, that I wish to speak for a few minutes. Like all legislative bodies, we do unwise things at times. I venture to say that we will do nothing more unwise this session than we will do if we pass this legislation, speaking from the standpoint of expediency alone. What are we doing? We are giving a company which is incorporated, not for patriotic purposes, not for the development of any portion of our territory, but for purely speculative and profitable purposes; and we are giving them without one dollar, a right to exploit our rivers, and to collect the latent energy that lies in those rivers, the enormous wealth those water-powers afford to the people of the province of Ontario, and this in face of the fact that the Whitney government have adopted a policy for developing this power throughout Ontario for the benefit of the people, which -we are handing over to a corporation to use for their own advantage; and worse than that, to export at least one-half of that power, at their will, into the territory of a foreign power, and by means of that exported energy to enable those people to build up rival institutions in the United States to the detriment of the Dominion of Canada- Mr. DEPUTY SPEAKER
that is what we are doing. From that standpoint I for one will oppose to the utmost this legislation and this class of legislation. I have no quarrel with my hon. friend. He and I have had some little passages, and with pleasure I have read the graphic accounts of it in the organ of the Minister of Agriculture, my hon. friend the ' Farmer;' I have read the manner in which I was raked fore and aft by my hon. friend, and how I was completely wiped out the other day. But all the same, I have no hard feelings towards my hon. friend, I am only trying to guard the interests of the people of Ontario and of the people of Canada. We are going to send abroad that which would be our capital at home, which would build up industries in our own country, which would afford occupation for our people, which would develop markets for every person in the country, markets for the farmer, markets for the butcher, markets for the baker, markets for the artisan, and employment for the doctor, and for that most deserving class of all, the lawyers, and work for all; and whilst we are robbing ourselves, we are doing the double injury to this country of building up rival institutions on the other side of the line. We can do nothing more insane than that. An hon. gentleman said to me to-night in conversation ' why, we have done it before.' Yes, we have done lots of unwise things before. I am ashamed to recollect that whilst I listened to that Bill going through, yet because I did not feel I could effectually oppose it, I let it go through virtually without protesting against it. But I venture to say we will be doing less than our duty if we allow any more of these Bills to go through. We should say in every case-and I appeal to the Prime Minister on this matter-that we will not allow any private corporation to develop power from the energy of our rivers, from that great wealth Providence has given us, and export that into foreign territory, with the result that our young men will have to go out and work in that foreign territory, and we shall be compelled to buy back the goods which should be manufactured within our own borders.
Now let me refer to what was said about this matter a year or two ago when this Bill was before parliament on a previous occasion. I think I mav say that whilst we are to form our own opinion about these matters, yet surely if we are to live iu harmony and work in harmony for the development of Canada, it ought to be the object of this parliament at Ottawa, as far as possible, to work in unison with the interests and the aims of the legislatures of the various provinces. Now, the Ontario government has developed and has set in

operation a great scheme for serving the people by means of the energy and the power latent in its water-powers. When the Bill was before the Canadian parliament to incorporate the Ontario and Michigan Power Company a year ago, Mr. Whitney introduced the following resolution in the Ontario legislature. After reciting the Bills, the resofution affirms:
That the effect of the proposed legislation will be to enable the company, without the consent of the province, to possess itself of valuable water privileges and powers owned by the province, and to export from Ontario the power generated by means of them.
That the proposed legislation will have the effect of preventing the province from utilizing, in accordance with its declared policy, the valuable water privileges and powers of the Pigeon, Nipigon and Sturgeon rivers for the benefit of the public, and will enable the proposed company to exploit them for private gain.
That this House views with alarm the repeated encroachments of the parliament of Canada on the rights of the province, and its efforts to withdraw from provincial jurisdiction and control works of a purely provincial character, and earnestly protests against such action, which this House believes to be contrary, if not to the letter, to the spirit of the British North America Act and to the intention of the framers.
That in the opinion of this House the proposed legislation would be an unwarranted and illegal interference with the territorial sovereignty of the province, and with its exclusive legislative authority under the British North America Act, and this House earnestly and firmly protests against the proposed Bill being given the form of law.
And this House hereby declares its readiness and determination

Remember that this resolution passed unanimously, Liberals as well as Conservatives supporting it.
And this House hereby declares its readiness and determination to support with all the means, constitutional and material, which it can command, the government of Ontario in taking such measures and proceedings as may be deemed requisite to assert, maintain and defend the legislative and territorial sovereignty of the province against all aggression and encroachment by the federal government and parliament, and if necessary in appealing to the imperial parliament for such amendments to the British North America Act as will safeguard the sovereignty of the provinces therefrom. It has been ruled this afternoon that we are not at liberty to quote here, for the benefit of hon. gentlemen, and in order to remind them of what they are forgetting, from editorials of the 'Globe.' But we cannot shut our eyes to the fact that the press of the country, the 'Globe' amongst other leading papers, are being aroused to the circumstance that members of this parliament, 143*
led by the right hon. gentleman, is receding far from their former declarations as to provincial rights, and that no people are more alarmed than the Liberals themselves at the attitude that the government has assumed in this regard. I am sincerely glad that, although there is not that evidence of complete amendment which we could desire, yet there is some evidence of improvement, of contrition, on the part of the government in the announcement made this afternoon by the Minister of Justice. We have been fighting strenuously against that iniquitous proposition which has been incorporated in so many Bills declaring, absolutely without evidence, that the enactment is for the general advantage of Canada. I am glad that the Minister of Justice, to-day, has to some extent come over to the views of the opposition by declaring that he cannot support that declaration in this charter. As regards the second clause he says that it is impossible to say that this is an enactment for the general advantage of Canada and that the clause should be struck out. In 1905 I find that Sir Wm. Mulock, in this House, enunciated sentiments somewhat along the same line, but I am sorry to say that the government has had a sad relapse since then. Sir Wm. Mulock said:
I think there is much in the observation of my hon. friend. The parliament of Canada has, in the past, been too careless in seizing, and usurping jurisdiction by declaring works to be for the general advantage of Canada without having some inquiry to justify that declaration.
We have been doing that and there is nothing fraught with greater danger to the maintenance of the proper relations between the provinces and the Dominion. There is nothing fraught with greater danger to the Dominion as a whole than in the parliament of Canada, with a strong hand, in defiance of fact and evidence and without justification, seizing to itself certain rights which it does not, in justice or in fact, possess, by merely making the bald declaration that the work is for the general advantage of Canada. We will have that provision eliminated from this Act. On the other hand, I ask the government at this stage to pause and consider whether some other policy, aside altogether from all technicality and keeping in view the best interests of Canada, with the object of conserving our great waterfalls for the development of the industrial interests of Canada, for the building up of enterprises within our own limits, and increasing our population and wealth should not be adopted. I would ask the government whether it is wise or expedient to permit a private corporation to have control of a great source of wealth such as this, to exploit it and to export it to a foreign land in rivalry with the industries of the people of Canada?

_ Mr. BARE. Mr. Chairman, it is not my intention to detain the committee with any extended remarks on this occasion, but I would not like to see this Bill, that I consider so important to this country, pass without entering my solemn protest against the interference with the rights of the province of Ontario which is involved in the measure. I do not think that any speaker on the other side of the House contended that this Bill does not enroach upon provincial rights. I was somewhat surprised at the speech of the Hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Aylesworth). Brilliant and strong as it was thought to be and as it was, and no doubt intended as it was to make an impression on this committee, I could not help noticing that he balanced and turned one way and the other to as great an extent as it was possible for him to do. I do not believe that he liked the task imposed upon him of defending so iniquitous a Bill as this one is. The only argument that he put forward in support of this Bill was that it had passed the committee, and he said that, in having passed the committee, this House should adopt it. I think that is the most dangerous doctrine that can be put forward. It would be a severe blow to the independence of this House if we were to consider that any Bill that had passed the railway or any other committee should go through this House in the form in which it had come from the committee. That committee is only intended to investigate and inquire, but it was never intended that the consideration of a Bill by the committee should ensure its passage through this House. What are the facts in connection with this Bill? If there was ever a Bill which had passed the Railway Committee which should receive careful consideration at the hands of this House it is the Bill which we have now before us. There are a number of the members of the committee who take a deep interest in the different Bills that come before it, but I am sorry to say-and I am not speaking of one side or the other-that there is a large quantiy of voting material available when it is required. Whenever a Bill is presented which is difficult to get through the committee and this House there is a certain amount of drumming up in order to fill the back seats of the committee-the smoking department of it-and the result is that when voting time comes these members are on hand to give their votes although many of them do not know anything of the merits or demerits of the Bill. This is a Bill in which the drumming up process was in evidence to a greater extent than in regard to any Bill which we have had before the committee this session. When this - Bill was before the Railway Committee, while we pointed to the iniquitous part of it, we had only to look around and see be-Mr. LENNOX.
hind the force that could vote down our objections, no matter what arguments we employed, no matter what position we took upon this great question that we consider of the utmost importance. It was under these circumstances that a vote was not insisted upon in the committee. We said: Let the Bill go through and throw the responsibility upon them. We could scarcely get in a remark because we could not occupy five minutes without such a noise being made behind us that we could not be heard. That was the Teason why we let this Bill go through, and it was not because we did not believe it was a most iniquitous measure. We believed that when the Bill came to this House there would be such a weakening of the support of those who were promoting it that it would not be possible for the measure to pass. It is not now so iniquitous as it was when it was before the committee. At that time we were convinced that it was so flagrant an attempt to violate the principle of provincial rights that it could not pass the House, but we are free to admit that the amendment which has been proposed makes a little improvement in it. Still the Bill is one which should not pass. Our water-powers are amongst the greatest assets we have. 'We can only look forward to the time when our water-powers must supply a want which no other resource in this country can supply. It is a well-known fact that year after year fires are sweeping away our forests and that our supply of coal in the lower provinces is becoming less. Under these circumstances I think it is a most unfortunate thing that we should alienate our natural resources. In looking over the history of the parliament of Canada and that of the province of Ontario, I think my hon. friend the member for Thunder Bay and Rainy River (Mr. Conmee) will agree with me when I say that as far as these natural resources are concerned my hon. friend has figured largely not only in this House but in the provincial House. I well remember in the dying days of the session of 1904 a fight over the Kakabeka falls when my hon. friend and his friends secured the Tight to that water-power from another company. We thought that was unjust and unfair, and there is no doubt that my hon. friend's action then alienated a large number of voters. The responsibility of that dying government seemed to be thrown upon my hon.* friend and he was deserted by his former friends as well as the Conservatives. The result was that the action of two year3 before was reversed, and that company is now going ahead under the control of other men. Now we find my hon. friend going along a different line.

I rise to a point of order. The hon. member states or insinuates that

I was one of the parties interested in the Kaministiquia Power Bill. The hon. member should withdraw that. I never had any interest direct or indirect in that Power Company.
